subject: radiology
title: Radiation Dosimetry: Absorbed Dose, Equivalent Dose, and Effective Dose

steps.title: Radioactivity and Disintegration Rates
steps.tx: **Becquerel radioactivity unit** serves as the standard SI measurement of nuclear activity, defined as exactly one spontaneous nuclear transformation or disintegration per second. It replaces the traditional non-SI unit, the curie, which was originally established as the radioactivity emitted by one gram of radium-226 and equals 3.7 multiplied by ten to the tenth becquerels.

steps.title: Radiation Exposure in Air
steps.tx: **Roentgen exposure measurement** quantifies the amount of electrical ionization produced by X-rays or gamma rays in a volume of dry air at standard temperature and pressure. One roentgen generates 2.58 multiplied by ten to the minus fourth coulombs of electrical charge per kilogram of air. Exposure measurements describe only radiation field strength, not energy deposited within human biological tissue.

steps.title: Absorbed Radiation Dose
steps.tx: **Gray absorbed dose unit** quantifies the physical energy deposited by ionizing radiation per unit mass of matter, defined as one joule of absorbed energy per kilogram of tissue. It supersedes the traditional legacy unit, the rad, which stood for radiation absorbed dose and represented 100 ergs per gram. Exactly one gray equals one hundred rads.

steps.title: Radiation Weighting Factors
steps.tx: **Radiation weighting factor** values normalize different radiation modalities according to their relative biological effectiveness and linear energy transfer. Photons, including diagnostic X-rays and gamma emissions, share a baseline weighting factor of 1. Electrons and beta particles also carry a factor of 1. In contrast, densely ionizing alpha particles and heavy fission fragments carry a factor of 20.

steps.title: Equivalent Dose Calculation
steps.tx: **Sievert equivalent dose** quantifies tissue-specific biological damage by multiplying the physical absorbed dose in grays by the radiation weighting factor. Expressed in sieverts, equivalent dose permits direct comparison of biological harm across disparate radiation types. For medical diagnostic X-rays with a weighting factor of 1, an absorbed dose of 1 gray produces an equivalent dose of exactly 1 sievert.

steps.title: Tissue Weighting Factors
steps.tx: **Tissue weighting factor distribution** reflects the relative susceptibility of individual organs to radiation-induced stochastic malignancy and hereditary harm, published under ICRP publication 103. Organs with the highest mitotic turnover, including red bone marrow, colon, lung, stomach, and female breast, each carry a weighting factor of 0.12. Across the entire human body, the sum of all tissue weighting factors equals 1.0.

steps.title: Effective Dose Calculation
steps.tx: **Effective dose calculation** estimates the overall stochastic risk to the entire human body when only specific organs are exposed. Calculated by summing the products of equivalent dose and corresponding tissue weighting factor for each irradiated organ, effective dose uses the sievert or millisievert unit. This metric allows clinicians to directly compare patient risk between localized examinations like head CT and general background exposure.

steps.title: Medical Imaging Versus Background Dose
steps.tx: **Natural background radiation comparison** places medical diagnostic exposures into realistic clinical perspective. Worldwide average natural background radiation delivers 2.4 to 3.0 millisieverts annually. A standard posteroanterior chest radiograph imparts approximately 0.02 millisieverts, equivalent to roughly three days of natural background. In contrast, an abdominal CT examination imparts 8 to 10 millisieverts, equivalent to three years of background radiation.
